title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Dementia—It's the Caregivers Who Get Dragged Down
dek: The hard part of dementia care isn't the patient's condition itself, but the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses, forces a post-90s worker to quit; love is the starting point but not the support, and the system hasn't caught up with these families.
why: This isn't elderly wellness science; it's a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia families: no standard answers, only realities you need to see before it's too late.
who: Post-80s and post-90s only children, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they've made no eldercare plans; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care gap eventually falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, 23% of the population; 35 million are disabled elderly, yet there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap isn't absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patients account for nearly 30% of the global total, and the host estimates that on average, one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this may be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies are unreliable
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia comes mostly from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the incontinence of the professor in 'Still Alice' is just one form. He met an elderly man who, despite dementia from his tailor background, would still notice stains on visitors' clothes and teach them to remove them with orange peel; and another who, after a car accident left him disabled, could only hum 'Liuyang River' with focused expression. Dementia encompasses Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, and other causes; each person's life imprint lingers differently, and care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal depends on state nursing insurance
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents live like residents, shopping at the supermarket and going to cafes, while staff pose as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose how hard it is to replicate: the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over 18 million euros, of which 17.8 million was covered by the government, and residents' costs are also covered by long-term care-related systems. In contrast, Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home that elevators had to be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease differs not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough; sacrifice drags down caregivers
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between 'I love my parents very much' and 'I'm about to be dragged down by them.' Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse must learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit due to caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers become patients too.

points.h: The more you see, the less prepared you feel for old age
points.body: After years of researching elder care, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his own parents' care. He is a first-generation only child; his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less confident he feels; his research assistant even said after each interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how to arrange her own parents' future. Multi-child families have friction too: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and one person who moved parents to Shenzhen found rent, medical costs, and nanny fees rising faster than retirement wages. The ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who initially could draw blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later could only praise others, afraid to put brush to paper; another woman's husband reported new losses weekly: his wife couldn't recognize their daughter's newborn grandson, not knowing where this child came from. This daily, irreversible downward slide drains caregivers more than physical disability. The long haul of care is not repetitive hardship but facing a small goodbye every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived but doesn't cover all elderly
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, expanded to about 90 cities by around 2025, with the official pace aiming for universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that it's not about giving money to every elderly person; through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care, meal delivery, and other services; those with mild conditions may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home is often equated with filial impiety in China, and elderly people, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair will fall out within a month. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the proportion choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap won't disappear on its own.

I think although love is a very important foundation, it shouldn't be the only condition for care. It still requires external resources, including social support, and so on.
